inputs.why: Crew language tendencies and base word rates.
Which crew and network call the game.
Storylines and events that trigger words.
Recent storylines that announcers will discuss.
Delays add airtime and topics.
Longer games add airtime: extra innings require a tie after nine innings; the probability depends on expected run totals and spread.
Postseason broadcasts differ in language.
Which feed, speakers and spoken vs displayed words count.
Market-implied probability and movement.
Historical realised frequency by word type.
The market is a Poisson-like exposure market with crew-specific rates; without these the probability is unanchored.
Converts a per-hour word rate into a per-game probability.
Name-based markets are driven by involvement, not by baseball skill statistics.

CONDITIONAL on contract text: only relevant if a future contract counts ad reads or sponsor segments; otherwise exclude it. Separates the deterministic scripted part of language from spontaneous commentary and respects counting rules.

interactions.hypothesis: Crew vocabulary x trigger events: the word probability is the crew's baseline rate plus a bump when the trigger event occurs, so trigger-event likelihood should be modelled separately.
Broadcast length x word rate: delays and extra innings lengthen the broadcast, so game-length uncertainty interacts with word rate.
Wording x feed: national vs local feeds differ and the contract defines the counted feed, so crew identity interacts with rules text.

P(at least one mention) = 1 - exp(-rate x hours) saturates in exposure for common words but is nearly linear for rare ones, so extending airtime by extras or delays matters only for words whose rate times hours is below about two. Crew determines the rate that sets which regime applies.

Topical words occur at baseline until a trigger fires, after which the rate jumps; the market probability is the mixture P(trigger) x P(word|trigger) + (1-P(trigger)) x baseline. Scheduled triggers (milestone chase, rivalry games) are visible pregame, but in-game triggers (no-hitter, injury) are not.

National versus local feed and counting rules (sponsors, graphics) switch the effective vocabulary; a contract limited to the national feed uses a different crew and sponsor mix than the home feed, so probability is determined first by the regime then by the rate. This holds only if a contract that counts ad reads exists (none in the ledger); treat as conditional.

A player's name rate multiplies his involvement (PA, pitching) and the storyline salience (return from injury, award talk); a star in a storyline gets a rate several times a bench player's, and a non-starter gets zero, so involvement gates the storyline effect.

Delays and extras both lengthen the broadcast but are nearly independent events with different tails; the airtime distribution is a convolution with a heavy right tail, so rare-word probabilities have a fat contribution from long-game scenarios.

announcer_mentions.label: Broadcast word-mention markets
announcer_mentions.mechanism: Mention probability reflects announcer vocabulary (crew-specific base rates), the length of the broadcast and events that trigger topics (milestones, pitching changes, weather delays, named players), with the contract's definition of which feed and what counts. Baseball statistics offer little direct signal, so this is closer to a novelty/language market with sparse history; the best hypotheses concern crew habits and trigger events.
announcer_mentions.target: Whether a specified word or phrase is spoken in the named broadcast, per the contract's source and counting rules.

inputs.why: Tied-after-nine rate by total/spread bucket.
Distribution shape drives P(tie).
Strong starters lower scoring and increase tie chance.
Late-inning scoring quality: relief pitchers' quality sets run prevention after the starter exits, determining full-game total and winner.
Low-scoring environments tie more.
Extra-inning strategy affects length of extras.
Historical delay rates and risk model.
Hourly precipitation and radar nowcast around first pitch.
Closed roof removes weather delay risk.
Lightning, wind and temperature.
Delay, suspension and postponement definitions.
Contract wording for extras and delay windows.
Market close vs actual first pitch time.
KXMLBEXTRAS settles on the tie event, so the joint distribution (not each team's total) is the right object.
Defines P(extras) as P(level score after nine complete innings) so both extras routes are included.
Distinguishes lightning-driven from rain-driven delays and sharpens the weather gate.
Defines the empirical event frequency and tests the sensitivity of the market to the recording threshold.

interactions.hypothesis: Total x spread: tie probability peaks when expected total is low and teams are evenly matched, so total and spread jointly drive extra-innings probability and should come from one run-distribution model.
Precipitation timing x roof state: the same forecast produces a delay only if the roof is open and the rain overlaps the game window, so roof state gates the weather risk.

Delay definition x time window: contracts counting only start delays are driven by pre-first-pitch weather, in-game delay contracts add game-length exposure (including extras), so the definition interacts with extra-innings probability.

Extras probability is the diagonal of the joint score distribution; shared park and weather push both teams' runs the same way, increasing diagonal mass at any given total. The effect is largest in extreme parks where the common factor is largest.

Delay probability is the product of weather overlapping the window and the roof being open; for retractable roofs the decision to close depends on forecast confidence, so closed-roof parks have near-zero delay, and the gating is a regime switch. Lightning adds delays on dry fields.
Extras equal tie after top 9 times failure to walk off; the failure probability depends on closer quality, so for elite closers the extras probability is lower for the same tie probability.

KXMLBDELAY's text counts in-game weather stoppages as well as a delayed start, so extra innings add weather exposure only while no start delay has been recorded; once any start delay occurs the market is already Yes and game length no longer matters. The dependence on extras is therefore conditional on the pre-game weather state.

Recorded delays follow a threshold in precipitation intensity and duration; light drizzle is played through while heavy rain triggers a tarp, so the response of delay probability to rain probability is steeply nonlinear above a threshold.

extras_and_delay.label: Extra innings and game delay/postponement
extras_and_delay.mechanism: Extra innings are the event that the two run totals tie after nine, so probability is a function of the run distribution (higher in low-total, close games) and of late-inning scoring, with the ghost runner shaping what happens after but not the event. Delay markets are weather-timing problems: probability of precipitation or lightning near first pitch relative to roof status and umpire/team decision behaviour, mostly independent of team quality. Both are low-to-moderate probability events decided by distributional shape and exact contract wording (start delay vs in-game delay, suspended-game treatment).
extras_and_delay.target: Whether the game goes to extra innings (tied after nine) or whether a delay/postponement occurs, per the contract definition.

inputs.why: Starter run prevention for innings 1-5.
Separation of starter vs bullpen run rates.
Probability of exit before the fifth inning.
Third time through the order raises run expectancy materially, so the starter's expected depth sets the first-five mean.
Lineup strength vs starter's hand.
Confirmed lineup: who bats and in what order determines the actual hitters a pitcher faces and the plate appearances each hitter gets.
Handedness composition: same-handed matchups favour pitchers (especially vs breaking balls), opposite-handed matchups favour hitters, and the size of the split differs by player.
Run environment: park dimensions, altitude and surface change run, HR and hit probabilities for both teams, and by batter handedness.
Weather: temperature, air density and wind change ball flight, so fly-ball outcomes (HR, doubles) vary with conditions.
Umpire zone for the early innings.
Contact allowed and defence: hits allowed depend on the quality of contact against a pitcher and the fielders converting it into outs.
Overdispersed F5 run distribution and tie probability.
Bullpen relevance in early exit cases.
Tie/push treatment and shortened-game rule for F5 markets.
ERA-minus-FIP gaps from stranding luck regress and mis-price first-five runs.
Without a refund clause the change risk is not hedged; it is a primary driver of early-market error.
Converts the confirmed lineup into five-inning exposure rather than a nine-inning average.
F5 differs from full game in how much bullpen enters; this is the explicit mixture weight.

interactions.hypothesis: Exit before the fifth: F5 run rate is a mixture of starter-only and bullpen-inclusive, so leash and bullpen state interact with starter quality.
Top-of-order exposure x handedness: in five innings the top of the lineup bats twice, so platoon quality of the top six hitters is weighted more than in a full game.
Tie handling x run distribution: F5 ties are common enough that push/loss rules change pricing; the discrete distribution and rule jointly define the probability.

F5 run rate is a mixture of starter-only innings and starter-plus-reliever innings: a good starter with a short leash pushes relievers into the fifth, while a mediocre starter with a long leash keeps them out, so the expected value depends on exit probability times the quality gap between starter and reliever.

Because slots 1-4 bat twice within five innings, platoon advantage at the top of the order is weighted more than in a full game; a lefty-heavy top four against a righty starter inflates F5 runs by more than the team-level wRC+ suggests. Tested at slot level as batter handedness (from the confirmed card) crossed with the starter hand, weighted by expected first-five PA, rather than against the duplicate platoon team aggregate.

The second-trip penalty arrives at about the 10th batter and is larger for pitchers with narrow arsenals, so the effect is discontinuous in batters faced and has a pitcher-specific size; strand luck regression changes how much of an early-inning performance the model attributes to the starter.

Tie handling and starter-change risk combine: a starter swap shifts the whole score distribution while the Tie strike pays on equal scores, so the joint PMF is a mixture over starter states with tie mass concentrated in low-total states.

The umpire zone matters most in low-offence environments where each walk is a bigger share of baserunners, and park/weather push toward the same margin; the interaction is a threshold in run environment where zone effects dominate pitcher's parks.

The F7 result depends on how many of innings six and seven each bullpen must cover and which relievers are available: a tired bullpen after an extra-inning game forces lower-leverage arms into the sixth, and a manager leading by a run uses setup men earlier, so the same starters imply different F7 distributions by bullpen state.

first5_markets.label: First-five-innings winner, spread and total
first5_markets.mechanism: Through five innings runs are scored mostly against the starters (typically two trips through the order), so the market is driven by starter quality, expected exit before the fifth, the lineups' strength against the starter's hand, and the environment, with the bullpen entering only after early exits. Relative to full game, bullpen strength is de-emphasised and starter leash risk is emphasised, and ties are possible so spread and winner contracts differ by tie handling.
first5_markets.target: First-five-innings result (winner/run spread) or total runs through five innings.

inputs.why: First-inning scoring distribution baseline.
The first three batters, not the whole lineup, decide the first inning.
Confirmed top-three hitters and order.
Handedness of top-order hitters vs starter.
Starter quality in the first trip through the order.
Early walks and zone rate: walks arise when pitchers miss the zone and hitters take pitches outside it; both the pitcher's command and the lineup's discipline matter.
K% reduces baserunners: strikeouts occur when a pitcher's swing-and-miss and called-strike ability meet hitters prone to striking out; lineup K% by handedness captures the hitter side.
First-three-innings pattern: the first three innings give every starter a full turn through the top of the order and are mostly pitcher-quality and lineup-top dependent.
Later-inning markets depend on trip through order.
Bullpen entry for later innings.
Run environment: park dimensions, altitude and surface change run, HR and hit probabilities for both teams, and by batter handedness.
Temperature and wind: temperature, air density and wind change ball flight, so fly-ball outcomes (HR, doubles) vary with conditions.
Early-game zone effect: the home-plate umpire's called zone determines strike/ball outcomes on borderline pitches, changing strikeouts, walks and run scoring.
Inning-level distribution: runs per team per game are overdispersed and inning-clustered, so threshold and total markets depend on distribution shape and the correlation between teams.
Rules for shortened/postponed games and extra innings in inning markets.
BABIP luck in the starter's recent first innings regresses; raw first-inning ERA overstates persistent skill.
Replaces first_inning_splits as a computational estimand and removes dependence on 30-start samples.
The ninth is a state-conditional, non-exchangeable inning; no existing catalog input captures the skipped-bottom and closer selection.
Provides the base rate by inning index and a ceiling for how much inning-specific tendency is real.

interactions.hypothesis: Top-three OBP x starter command: first-inning scoring requires baserunners from top hitters against the starter's zone and walk rate, so the product by half-inning and the two-half-inning union give the event probability.

Handedness x starter first-trip arsenal: lefty-heavy top order against a righty with a weak changeup changes first-inning run probability beyond aggregate wRC+, so platoon should be applied to the top three.
Small-sample first-inning splits x PA-level simulation: observed first-inning ERA is mostly noise, so it should enter only as a heavily shrunk adjustment to the PA-level model.

A run in the first inning requires baserunners from the top three and then enough extra-base power or walks to convert, so the probability depends on the product of leadoff on-base skill, the number-three hitter's power and the pitcher's walk rate rather than their sum. A lineup top with two high-OBP hitters against a command-poor starter compounds.

The ninth-inning run distribution has three regimes: save situation with closer (low run probability), tied or one-run with high-leverage arms, and blowout with mop-up arms; home-bats flag changes whether the bottom exists. The regime probabilities come from the score distribution, so ninth-inning markets are a mixture priced by margin.

Whether the ninth is played at all, and how many runs it can contain, depends on the margin entering the bottom half: a home lead removes it, a tie or one-run deficit ends it at the go-ahead run, and the due-up hitters set how often that run arrives. The truncation lowers over-1.5 and Tie-strike probabilities relative to the untruncated half-inning run distribution, most for tied games with a high-OBP due-up group.

Platoon advantage of the top of the order is conditional on the starter's pitch arsenal: a lefty-heavy top against a right-hander with a good changeup differs from the same top against a slider-only right-hander; the effect is realised in the first trip where hitters have not adjusted.

The KXMLBINNINGWIN tie strike is a joint event of top- and bottom-9th runs: when the home team leads it equals P(visitors score 0 against the home closer or setup man); when tied or trailing the home half is truncated at the winning run, so a 1-1 or 2-2 ninth is rarer than independent half-innings imply and 0-0 dominates. The weight on each case comes from the margin distribution entering the ninth and from which relievers are available.

first_inning_and_inning_markets.label: First-inning runs and inning-level markets
first_inning_and_inning_markets.mechanism: An inning is a short Markov process through base-out states with outcomes depending on the three hitters due up and the pitcher on the mound; for the first inning the top three of each lineup face the fresh starter, so the run probability (YRFI) is the union of two half-innings with probabilities driven by top-order on-base skill, handedness and starter first-trip command. Later-inning markets additionally depend on which batters are due, TTO penalty and bullpen entry, which are partly unknowable pregame. Small samples make historical first-inning splits mostly noise; PA-level simulation is preferred.
first_inning_and_inning_markets.target: Whether runs are scored in a specific inning (first inning or other inning), which team outscores the other in the inning, or the inning's run total.

Expected innings determine starter vs bullpen weight.
Confirmed lineup strength vs starter handedness.
Lineup confirmation and rest-day sit-downs.
Availability/fatigue of relievers.
Reliever quality: relief pitchers' quality sets run prevention after the starter exits, determining full-game total and winner.
Defence and framing: fielders convert balls in play to outs at different rates; catchers add or steal strikes, changing both BABIP and K/BB.
Run environment: park dimensions, altitude and surface change run, HR and hit probabilities for both teams, and by batter handedness.
Weather and wind: temperature, air density and wind change ball flight, so fly-ball outcomes (HR, doubles) vary with conditions.
Umpire zone effect: the home-plate umpire's called zone determines strike/ball outcomes on borderline pitches, changing strikeouts, walks and run scoring.
Late scratches and IL moves: absences change lineup/rotation composition and late scratches can void or reprice player markets.
Travel and schedule: fatigue and travel affect position players' availability, starters' rest and bullpen usage.
Regress luck in team record: team records deviate from run-differential-based expectations because of sequencing, one-run games and bullpen luck, and deviations mean-revert.
Run-difference distribution for spread and margin.
Extra-innings resolution of ties.
Opponent-adjusted team strength.
Sharp-line benchmark: sharp sportsbook and exchange lines are a competing aggregation of information and the standard benchmark for fair probability.
Move after lineup/starter news.
Postponement, suspended game and extras settlement.
The lineup's handedness mix against the starter shifts run expectancy by several percent.
Starter pitch mix against the lineup's pitch-type weaknesses changes strikeout and contact quality.
Confirmed-lineup strikeout rate by handedness is the market-free matchup summary available after lineups post.
Late lineup news is the main non-market source of game-level edge and has no explicit measured input in the catalog beyond a data feed.
Distinguishes between parks with large and small HFA, and handles walk-off truncation correctly for margin strikes.
Distribution tail for run-line and margin contracts, as sketched in the existing run_dist hypothesis but without a measured input.
Fills the regular-season motivation gap for KXMLBGAME-type contracts (late-season starts, rested regulars) that rest_travel and series_context do not address.
KXMLBSTGAME requires a team-strength measure for the players who actually play spring innings and the tie probability the contract does not address.

interactions.hypothesis: Starter innings x bullpen gap: the effective edge from a better starter equals quality gap times expected innings, plus bullpen gap times remaining innings, so workload and bullpen quality should be combined into a weighted pitching rating.

Confirmed lineup x starter handedness x arsenal: lineup strength should be platoon- and pitch-type-specific, so a rested star or lefty-heavy lineup against a righty changes team strength beyond season wRC+.

Run-line cover depends on distribution: favourites win by 2+ less often than win probability suggests because of one-run games and bullpen use when ahead, so margin should come from the run distribution and late-game leverage.
Lineup/starter confirmation timing x price: markets open before lineups, so the edge is how fast the model reprices on confirmation relative to the quote history.

The effective pitching edge is the starter quality gap times the share of innings he covers plus the bullpen gap times the rest, so starter workload acts as a weight that changes with the specific starter and with postseason leashes. A better starter who goes five innings counts for less than the same gap over seven.

Confirmed-lineup changes matter conditional on the starter's hand and the slot of the missing hitter: a left-handed bat resting against a lefty starter is no loss, while a missing right-handed regular against a lefty is. The same absence has different run value by matchup.

Home advantage concentrates in the late innings: home teams skip the bottom 9th when ahead and win tied games by last bat, so HFA enters margin strikes as truncation and win probability as a tie-resolution bonus, not as a uniform shift in run difference.

Large margins are compressed because trailing teams' pitchers are replaced with weaker arms only after the game is out of reach, while narrow leads are protected; the probability of covering a 1.5-run spread is therefore not monotone with a constant-variance model, and fatigued bullpens loosen the compression.

In a postseason single game the series state switches bullpen and starter usage: in elimination games the best relievers pitch more and earlier and starters are pulled at the first sign of trouble, so a starter-quality edge counts for fewer innings and the late-inning margin distribution tightens; in non-elimination games of a lopsided series usage relaxes.

In spring the announced starter's quality matters only for his planned two to four innings, after which depth arms of unknown quality pitch; the effect of a better starter on win probability is therefore cut off at his innings limit, unlike the regular season where an ace's influence extends six or more innings.

game_moneyline.label: Game winner, run line and winning margin
game_moneyline.mechanism: Win probability is built from expected run scoring and prevention for each team at the plate-appearance level: starter quality and expected innings, bullpen quality and availability, confirmed lineup quality against the starter's hand and arsenal, defence, park and weather and the umpire's zone, with a modest home-field effect. The win probability is a function of the run-difference distribution (overdispersed, with extra-innings resolution of ties), so run line and margin contracts need the full distribution rather than the moneyline alone. Late information (confirmed lineups, scratched starters, weather/roof) is the main edge source, and records must be regressed to run-based talent.
game_moneyline.target: Which team wins the game (including extra innings unless worded otherwise), covers a run spread, or wins by a particular margin.

inputs.why: Both starters' run prevention.
Starter innings vs bullpen exposure.
Fatigue and availability for the late innings.
Reliever run prevention: relief pitchers' quality sets run prevention after the starter exits, determining full-game total and winner.
Lineup offence by handedness: a team's lineup quality against the starter's handedness determines runs in the early innings, more than overall season team offence.
Confirmed lineup: who bats and in what order determines the actual hitters a pitcher faces and the plate appearances each hitter gets.
Run factors: park dimensions, altitude and surface change run, HR and hit probabilities for both teams, and by batter handedness.
Wind and temperature: temperature, air density and wind change ball flight, so fly-ball outcomes (HR, doubles) vary with conditions.
Wind component relative to park axis.
Carry changes: lower air density reduces drag and increases ball carry, raising HR and scoring (Denver, hot days).
Roof open/closed controls weather effect.
Zone effect: the home-plate umpire's called zone determines strike/ball outcomes on borderline pitches, changing strikeouts, walks and run scoring.
Contact allowed and defence: hits allowed depend on the quality of contact against a pitcher and the fielders converting it into outs.
Fielding and catcher framing: fielders convert balls in play to outs at different rates; catchers add or steal strikes, changing both BABIP and K/BB.
Regress BABIP in team samples.
League run environment: league-wide rule and equipment changes shift league baselines for steals, BABIP, pace and run scoring between seasons.
Overdispersion and tail shape.
Extra innings add runs where counted.
Total and team total rungs consistency.
Counting of extra innings, shortened and suspended games.
Directly changes total thresholds near the median, especially for strong home favorites, and is absent from the existing catalog.

The existing catalog assumes extras count but the sampled rules are silent; the input keeps the dependence explicit and testable. Re-specified by regime because all sampled totals are postseason games, where the automatic runner is not used to my knowledge.
KXMLBSERIESGAMES settles directly on series length; no catalog input models it.

interactions.hypothesis: Wind x air density x park: HR/fly-ball effects are multiplicative in HR-friendly parks, so weather adjustments should be computed from deviations from park norms and interacted with park HR factor and fly-ball tendencies.
Starter exit x bullpen state: totals are a mixture of starter and bullpen run rates by inning, so starter workload and bullpen availability/quality interact to give the late-inning scoring.
Umpire zone x walk-prone pitcher/lineup: a small zone raises totals most when a pitcher is walk-prone and lineups are patient, so umpire effects should depend on plate-discipline matchup.
Dispersion x threshold: high-total and low-total rungs price tails; park and weather affect variance as well as mean (Coors, wind games), so dispersion should depend on environment.

Park factor, wind and air density multiply the same fly-ball carry, so in a hitter's park with a tailwind and thin air the effects compound; deviations from park norms, not absolute weather, carry the information, and the effect is largest for fly-ball-heavy lineups and starters.

The total is a mixture of starter-run and bullpen-run innings, so the sensitivity of the total to starter quality depends on how long he goes, which depends on bullpen state and leash. A depleted bullpen lengthens the leash and thereby increases weight on the starter's quality.

A smaller called zone raises walks and run scoring most for patient lineups against command-poor pitchers, and a larger zone helps pitchers with edge-heavy approach; umpire effect scales with the matchup's walk exposure rather than adding a fixed number of runs.

In high-run environments variance rises faster than the mean (clustering of crooked-number innings), so the probability of totals above the model median falls less than a constant-variance model implies, and the under side is more exposed at low thresholds.

Game-length regime: when the home team leads, the bottom of the ninth is skipped (negative total adjustment); when tied, extras add runs; when the home team trails, the game runs to completion. The three regimes sit at different parts of the run-difference distribution, so the expected total is a mixture with different slopes.

game_total_and_team_total.label: Game total and team total runs
game_total_and_team_total.mechanism: Expected runs = sum over plate appearances of per-PA run value for each team, driven by starter quality over the innings he pitches, bullpen run rate for the rest, the lineups' quality by handedness, and multiplicative park/weather/air-density and umpire effects; the realised distribution is overdispersed and inning-clustered so thresholds price tail probabilities. Team totals isolate one offence against the opposing pitching staff and defence. The main edges are late environmental/lineup information (wind, roof, confirmed lineup, scratched starter) and correct dispersion and regression of luck.
game_total_and_team_total.target: Whether total runs (or one team's runs) exceed a threshold under the contract's scope (including extra innings, shortened game rules).

inputs.why: Lineup slot and game script set plate appearances; pinch-hitting and blowout substitution cut them.
Confirmed slot and participation define PAs.
True-talent per-PA outcome rates with projections.
xBA/xSLG and barrel% predict hits/TB beyond results.
Handedness split against starter and bullpen.
Hitter's pitch-type performance against the starter's arsenal.
Starter quality affects first two or three PAs.
Starter's contact suppression and defence behind him.
Relief quality for late PAs: relief pitchers' quality sets run prevention after the starter exits, determining full-game total and winner.
Park hit and TB factors by handedness.
Weather influences extra-base hit rates.
Speed influences infield hits and extra bases.
Regress BABIP luck: batting average on balls in play deviates from what contact quality and defence imply, and the deviation mostly reverts.
Small, shrunk correction for role/injury changes.
Compound distribution for threshold probabilities.
RBI component of H+R+RBI needs runners ahead.
Runs component needs on-base skill and hitters behind.
Appearance requirement and voids.
Hits and TB rungs for one hitter are nested and linked.
A 3+ hit rung needs a third and often fourth PA, so the truncation survival to PA4 is a first-order determinant.
Total bases and hits for left-handed hitters against righty starters depend materially on the likelihood of facing a left-handed reliever later.
Distinguishes a singles hitter from a power hitter with the same xBA, which matters for the 2+/3+/4+ total-bases rungs.

interactions.hypothesis: PA count x per-PA probability: expected hits = expected PA x P(hit per PA); the lineup slot and team total shift PA while contact quality shifts probability, so both must be in one compound model.
Platoon x pitch-type matchup: same-handed breaking-ball-heavy starters suppress hitters with weak breaking-ball performance, so platoon and pitch-mix effects interact rather than add.
Contact quality x defence/park: expected TB depends on how hard and where a hitter hits the ball relative to park dimensions and fielders, so xSLG should be park- and defence-adjusted.
BABIP luck x recent form: recent hot hitting driven by BABIP should not move the projection, so recent form should enter through contact quality, not batting average.

A 3+ hit rung needs at least three PAs and realistically four, so its probability is a step-like function of the PA distribution: replacing the fifth PA with a pinch hitter moves P(3+ hits) little while losing the fourth moves it a lot. The PA distribution, not the mean, interacts with per-PA hit probability. Stated on the PA-count survival vector crossed with the per-PA hit/total-base probability from the batted-ball outcome model.

Platoon advantage flips between the starter and later relievers, so the batter's per-PA probability is conditional on pitcher hand by PA index; a lefty hitter vs a righty starter may face two lefty relievers late, offsetting the early advantage. Pitch-type specifics add little on top of hand.

Total bases depend on the product of contact quality, park gap/wall geometry and runner speed on doubles and triples; a hard-hit line drive in a deep-gap park by a fast runner is worth more than the same ball elsewhere. Park factors for doubles/triples must be applied to the hitter's spray profile, not league-average park multipliers.

In blowouts regulars on the leading team are removed early (PA lost) while on the trailing team they bat to the end; the game-script regime therefore changes both team strength and the hitter's PA, in opposite directions across the two teams.

H+R+RBI counts the same events multiple times, so the components are positively correlated through team scoring and inning clustering; the sum's variance is greater than the sum of component variances. A hitter's own hit adds to all three when he scores and drives himself in.

hitter_hits_and_total_bases.label: Hitter hits, total bases and hits+runs+RBIs thresholds
hitter_hits_and_total_bases.mechanism: Hits and total bases are sums over plate appearances of per-PA outcome probabilities (single, double, triple, HR vs out), so the expected value is expected PAs (lineup slot, team scoring, substitution risk) times per-PA rates and the distribution is a compound binomial/multinomial. Per-PA rates combine the hitter's contact quality, K and BB, platoon, pitch-type matchup against the starter, park and weather, defence, and later the bullpen; BABIP luck regresses. H+R+RBI adds team-dependent components (runners ahead, hitters behind), increasing variance and correlation with team scoring.
hitter_hits_and_total_bases.target: Whether a hitter records at least k hits, total bases or H+R+RBI in the game, requiring appearance per the wording.

inputs.why: Barrel%, pull-air%, FB% and max EV predict HR beyond past HR totals.
Bat speed/squared-up rate adds a stabilising early power signal.
Barrel and hard-hit rates supplement the HR profile.
Pitcher's HR/FB, barrels and fly-ball rate allowed by hand.
Park HR factor by handedness and ball carry environment.
Wind out/in component along the hitter's pull side.
Temperature/humidity/altitude change carry.
Handedness matchup influences HR rate.
Fastball-hitter vs fastball-heavy pitcher matchup.
PA multiplier by slot and team total.
Confirmed lineup and slot: who bats and in what order determines the actual hitters a pitcher faces and the plate appearances each hitter gets.
Later PAs face relievers with different HR vulnerability.
Regress hot/cold HR/FB luck: home runs per fly ball regress strongly to a mean determined by park and contact quality, so past HR luck is not persistent.
1+ and 2+ HR rungs are nested and linked to total HR environment.
Appearance requirement and settlement for postponed/shortened games.
Per-PA home-run probability, compounded over expected PAs, gives the any-HR probability; park, wind and pitcher enter per PA.
Barrel-driven hitters have heavier tails than a constant per-PA rate implies.
Connects hitter spray profile to day-specific carry, a more exact form of the park-by-wind interaction than separate factors.
Team bullpen_talent (xFIP) conflates K/BB with HR; the HR-specific relief exposure is what matters here.
Series HR contracts are priced on exposure, not just per-game HR rate.
Calibrates the 2+ HR rung and joint HR outcomes consistently.
Gives the live KXMLBWALKOFFS contract an explicit exposure-times-rate input; without it the series has no required inputs at all.

interactions.hypothesis: Hitter pull-air profile x park pull-side HR factor x wind: HR probability depends on the hitter's spray direction relative to the park's short side and the wind along that line, so the three should be modelled jointly.
Barrel rate x pitcher HR vulnerability x pitch type: HR risk is highest when a hitter's strong pitch type meets a pitcher who throws it in the damage zone, so matchup is by pitch type and zone.
Air density x wind x park: warm, thin air plus out-blowing wind in a short-porch park compound, but are already partially included in park factors, so use deviation from park norms.
PA count x per-PA HR rate: because per-PA HR probability is small, extra PA from batting slot or team scoring matters almost linearly, interacting with lineup posting and substitution risk.

A pull-power hitter's HR probability is the product of his pull-air barrel rate, the park's wall geometry on that side and the wind component along that line; each alone is mild but together they move per-PA probability by factors of two. The spray direction links the hitter profile to the specific wind and wall, so they must be modelled jointly.

Per-PA HR probability changes mid-game as the starter is replaced: PAs 1-3 use the starter's vulnerability, PAs 4-5 the reliever's. A homer-prone starter who is pulled early shifts exposure to a different arm, so total HR expectation is a PA-weighted mix conditioned on exit time.

Carry gains from thin air and tailwind add to the park norm but saturate near the wall: a ball that clears by feet gains nothing from more carry while a ball at the warning track gains most. The joint effect is therefore concave in the sum of wind and density and strongest for borderline fly balls.

HRs of hitters in the same game share weather and pitcher-day factors, so P(2+) and any multi-hitter outcome has positive dependence; the 2+ rung for one hitter is sensitive to the shared factor and to his PA count in the extra-inning tail.

The 2+ rung needs two home runs, so it is convex in the number of plate appearances: a leadoff hitter in a game with high projected team runs who stays in for a fifth PA has a disproportionately higher P(2+) than a bottom-order hitter at risk of being pinch-hit for late, while P(1+) moves almost linearly. Power hitters are rarely pinch-hit for, so the truncation risk concentrates in platoon and defensive players.

hitter_home_runs.label: Hitter home runs (1+ / 2+)
hitter_home_runs.mechanism: HR per game = 1 - product over PAs of (1 - p_HR), where per-PA HR probability multiplies the hitter's fly-ball/pull/barrel profile by the pitcher's HR vulnerability (by handedness and pitch type), the park's handedness-specific HR factor and the weather (wind component, temperature/air density). Because the base probability is low, multiplicative environment shifts matter and the dominant uncertainty is Bernoulli luck; HR/FB regresses to a contact-quality-determined mean. PA count (batting slot) and the bullpen's HR vulnerability also matter.
hitter_home_runs.target: Whether a hitter hits at least one (or two) home runs in the game, requiring appearance per the wording.

inputs.why: OBP of preceding hitters and team run environment set RBI chances.
Slot, teammates on base and score state set the opportunity count.
Confirmed slot and surrounding hitters.
Power and contact skill converts runners into RBIs.
Team offence against the starter's hand sets baserunner volume.
Starter quality determines baserunners and run scoring.
Relievers for later PAs: relief pitchers' quality sets run prevention after the starter exits, determining full-game total and winner.
Run environment: park dimensions, altitude and surface change run, HR and hit probabilities for both teams, and by batter handedness.
Steal attempt context: pitcher hold time, catcher pop time.
Runner attempt and success rates.
Sprint speed drives attempts and success.
Rule changes shifted SB attempt and success baselines.
Manager aggressiveness and platoon/pinch-hit style.
Runs depend on on-base skill and hitters behind.
Count distribution for RBI thresholds.
Appearance requirement and SB/CS scoring definitions.
Rungs for the same player share latent opportunity.
Exact RBI-opportunity input for the lineup and opponent; avoids averaging slot opportunity over lineups.
Separates opportunity from conversion so the model knows why a hitter has RBIs; avoids regressing noisy RISP batting average.
Provides an exact per-game decomposition for the 1+ steals ladder instead of season SB rate times PA.
Gives the batting-behind effect on RBI opportunity and stolen-base decisions a measured input instead of leaving it only in an interaction.

interactions.hypothesis: RBI opportunity x power: RBI = (runners on base when batting) x (conversion given hitter), so on-base skill of preceding batters should multiply the hitter's extra-base and contact skill rather than add.

SB attempt: runner speed x pitcher hold time x catcher arm x game state; each factor changes both attempt and success and they must be combined (a slow pitcher with a weak catcher invites attempts by fast runners).
Reaching base x attempt: P(SB) requires the runner to reach first or second, so OBP and expected PA interact with attempt rate, making lineup slot critical.
Rule regime x manager style: the post-2023 rules raised attempts, but managers differ in green-light rates, so regime baselines should be interacted with team style.

RBIs are runners on base times conversion given runners, so a hitter with elite conversion but poor lineup context and a hitter with ordinary conversion in an on-base-heavy lineup can have similar expected RBIs. The product, not a sum, is the right structure, and zero-runner PAs contribute no RBI except a solo home run.

Steal probability is opportunity times attempt hazard times success; slow pitchers and weak-armed catchers raise both attempt and success for fast runners but have little effect on slow runners, so the battery effect scales with runner speed and manager green light.

The post-2023 rules (bigger bases, pickoff limits) switched league SB attempt and success levels, and teams differ in how much their managers adapted; a model must reset the baseline at the regime boundary and let manager style scale it.

The batter behind a runner affects both RBI opportunity and the steal decision: a strong hitter behind a speedster makes managers less likely to send him early, while a weak batter behind raises steal probability. The lineup order therefore conditions both ladders in opposite ways.

P(2+ RBI) is convex in the game run environment, which here is carried by the team run-scoring opportunity (rbi_opportunity) shifted by park and opposing starter: low-total games almost never produce 2+ while high-total games do so disproportionately. It is convexity, not a threshold, and uses no market total.

hitter_rbis_runs_sb.label: Hitter RBIs, runs scored and stolen bases
hitter_rbis_runs_sb.mechanism: RBI depend on the number of runners on base when the hitter bats (OBP of hitters ahead, team scoring) and the hitter's ability to drive them in (power, contact, situational), so they are heavily context-dependent and high-variance, with lineup slot and team total dominating. Stolen bases require reaching base, deciding to attempt (runner speed, manager, game state) and succeeding against the pitcher's hold time and the catcher's arm, a low-frequency event with rule-regime shifts (pickoff limits, bigger bases). Both markets depend on lineup confirmation and on the opposing starter and catcher.
hitter_rbis_runs_sb.target: Whether a hitter records at least k RBIs or stolen bases in the game (runs and combos via H+R+RBI are in the hits archetype), requiring appearance per the wording.

inputs.why: Reference-class frequency: for off-field markets, history of similar announcements is the best available prior.
Timestamped reports: transactions and news change who plays and the team's strength with a lag before statistics catch up.
Transaction calendar where relevant.
Resolution wording and source.
Price reaction to news: the traded price aggregates every participant's information about this contract, including injury and lineup news that moves faster than public stats.
Liquidity affects quote reliability.
Close time vs event timing: market open, close, halts and postponement events determine when information can be traded on and which pregame snapshot is the last valid one.
Other venues' prices where they exist.
Base rates by market type: realized frequency by rung gives the unconditional base rate that every conditional model must beat, and reveals persistent biases in how thresholds are set.
Gives a concrete quantity for the voter model rather than a generic base rate.
KXMLBTEAMSALE settles only on finalization and approval, so stage and duration drive the probability.
Provides the only relevant information for the esports contract and keeps baseball features from contaminating it.
Gives KXMLBCOACH an identity-level selection input; without it the series had no mechanism beyond a generic hazard.
KXMLBFODTEAMS resolves all clubs No if no 2027 game is announced with participants or played, so staging is the first multiplier.
Gives each KXMLBFODTEAMS club market a probability that respects the two-participant constraint and regional selection pattern.

interactions.hypothesis: Base rate x time remaining: hazard concentrates around known dates, so base rates must be time-conditioned by the market window.
News timing x resolution source: reports precede official announcements, so price reaction must be read against what the rules count.
Thin liquidity x price moves: sparse trading makes quotes noisy, so volume interacts with moves to separate information from noise.

A club's Yes probability is P(game staged) times its marginal in the pair choice; news that strengthens one club's selection does nothing if the event itself is doubtful, and a staging confirmation lifts every plausible club at once while leaving their ratios unchanged.

Under a lockout after Dec 1 2026 the 2027 schedule is not finalised, so selection cannot be announced and the event may be dropped; if the market closes before a delayed release the all-No branch applies, so labour risk matters more the earlier the close date.

A report naming a pairing moves club probabilities in proportion to the outlet's reliability for schedule leaks; local reports about hotel blocks or permits for specific dates are informative only if the clubs scheduled that week match the leaked pairing.

Clubs beyond a few hundred miles of eastern Iowa have near-zero selection probability unless they are a national draw, so the distance effect is a threshold rather than a smooth decline, and the generic off-field base rate overstates distant clubs.

offfield_markets.label: Business, non-baseball and esports novelty markets
offfield_markets.mechanism: These markets are driven by organisational decisions and external events rather than on-field performance. There is little statistical structure: the best-supported hypotheses are reference-class frequencies, calendar constraints and timestamped news relative to the resolution wording. Non-baseball and esports items are not predicted by baseball inputs at all and should be treated as novelty markets with no baseball model.
offfield_markets.target: Events outside baseball games settled by public announcement or defined sources.

inputs.why: Batters faced multiplier for all three stats.
Exit time bounds the number of batters faced and therefore every count stat.
Contact quality allowed and defence behind the pitcher drive hits and runs.
Pitcher command vs lineup chase and walk rates drive walks.
Lineup quality vs pitcher's handedness for hits and runs.
Confirmed lineup replaces probable lineups.
HR risk is the biggest driver of earned run tails.
Regress BABIP to expected for hits.
Regress strand rate for earned runs.
Umpire zone changes walks and runs.
Framing affects walks: a catcher who gets more borderline pitches called strikes raises the pitcher's strikeout and lowers walk rates.
Strikeouts remove baserunner chances.
Ground-ball pitchers allow fewer extra-base hits.
Fielders convert balls in play to outs.
Park run and hit factors: park dimensions, altitude and surface change run, HR and hit probabilities for both teams, and by batter handedness.
Weather and wind shift hits and HR.
Inherited runners charged to the starter depend on bullpen.
Starter requirement, definitions of earned runs and scoring changes.
Threshold rungs for the three stats are internally nested.
A plate-appearance simulation produces the full distribution of hits, walks and earned runs from matchup probabilities.
Counts are over-dispersed; ignoring that mis-prices the tails of ladder thresholds.
Provides the conversion from hits and walks ladders to the earned-runs ladder without relying on a regressed LOB% alone.

Earned runs ladder differs from the runs distribution by this share; rungs at 3+ and 4+ move materially on a bad defense. Category reflects a fielding/defence quantity (errors and passed balls) rather than an official judgement, though the earned/unearned split is an official-scorer rule.
Needed for the ER tail rungs where blow-ups leave a crowded base path.
Hits allowed is a scorer-decided count; tendencies shift rungs slightly and can flip close settlements.
Adds the missing 2026 zone-regime driver to the walks ladder and to baserunner volume for ER.

interactions.hypothesis: Hits = balls in play x hit rate: K% and BB% determine balls in play, contact quality and defence determine conversion, so strikeout and contact profiles must be combined, not treated as independent.
Walks: pitcher zone rate x lineup chase/patience x umpire zone x framing; each is modest but together can move walk probability materially for command-poor pitchers.
Earned-run tail: HR vulnerability x park/wind x hook; early HR-driven blow-ups cause pulls, truncating but fattening the middle of the distribution.
Luck regression: observed BABIP and LOB% revert, so expected hits and earned runs use xBABIP and FIP-style run estimators with sample-weighted shrinkage.

Hits equal balls in play times hit probability, and balls in play are batters faced minus strikeouts, walks and home runs. A high-strikeout pitcher therefore has lower exposure to BABIP luck and a pitcher with a high BABIP-against can still be low on hits if he strikes batters out, so the effect of contact quality is scaled by the share of PAs that reach play.

Walk probability per PA rises convexly with the number of borderline balls called, because full counts compound: a smaller called zone and a poor framer push more counts to 3-ball, and each added ball increases the chance of a walk non-linearly. Command-poor pitchers against patient lineups are most exposed. In 2026 the zone is partly overridden by ABS challenges, so umpire and framing coefficients are estimated with a regime flag.

A home run costs one run plus the number of runners aboard, so expected earned runs from HR vulnerability grows convexly with traffic; HR-friendly parks and wind raise the probability that traffic is cleared. The ER ladder at 4+ is dominated by this joint of traffic and HR, not by average HR rate.

If the starter is pulled with runners on base, part of his final earned runs depends on which reliever enters and how fresh the bullpen is. The hook and the bullpen jointly create a conditional addition to ER that is largest in exactly the outings that already ended badly.

When an error or passed ball extends an inning, the scorer reconstructs the inning and later runs become unearned, so ER switches regime from tracking runs to lagging them. Teams with weak infield defense or a passed-ball catcher spend more time in the second regime.

pitcher_earned_runs_hits_walks.label: Starting pitcher earned runs, hits allowed and walks allowed
pitcher_earned_runs_hits_walks.mechanism: All three are batters faced times a per-PA event rate, but with different structure: hits depend on contact quality, defence and BABIP luck with K and BB removing balls in play; walks depend on the pitcher's command versus the lineup's patience and on the umpire zone and framing; earned runs add sequencing (LOB%, HR) on top of baserunners and truncate with the hook. The three are positively correlated within a start through shared latent command and contact quality and negatively with outs/strikeouts. Luck components (BABIP, LOB%, HR/FB) are large and regress, so expected-rate models beat observed outcomes.
pitcher_earned_runs_hits_walks.target: Whether the starter allows at least k earned runs, hits or walks in the game, requiring the pitcher to start per the wording.

inputs.why: Expected batters faced/pitch count distribution is the primary driver of outs.
Manager hook tendencies and score/bullpen contingencies determine early-exit probability.
Rehab, return and workload caps create hard ceilings on outs.
Pitches per out (low P/PA, high first-pitch strike) lets pitchers record more outs per 100 pitches.
Patient lineups raise pitches per out.
Run-prevention quality lowers blow-up risk that triggers early hooks.
Contact allowed and defence drive on-base events per BF.
Walks are pitch-expensive non-outs.
Strikeouts are outs but cost pitches; interplay with efficiency.
Third-trip penalty raises on-base rate and pull probability.
Velocity loss predicts shorter outing.
Rest and last start's pitch count affect stamina and cap.
Short or tired bullpen lengthens the leash; fresh bullpen shortens it.
Openers and bullpen games make the listed pitcher's outs very small.
Postseason hooks are shorter, moving outs distribution.
Heat and delays affect stamina and manager decisions.
Run environment influences blow-up risk.
Starter requirement and handling of partial innings, delays and voids.
Outs rungs at 15/18/21 outs are strongly nested and share a workload latent.
The ladder is lattice-valued; managers' inning-completion habits decide whether neighbouring rungs are priced near-equal or far apart.
Directly converts the batters-faced distribution into outs; a pitcher with 24 BF and 4 DP outs gets 3 more outs than 'one out per out-batter' implies.
Rain is the one interruption that changes outs without any pitching information.
Supplies the opposing-offence driver of outs per batter faced, which the pitcher-only inputs lacked.
Replaces the circular claim that the zone effect is already inside pitches per PA by modelling the 2026 regime shift explicitly.

interactions.hypothesis: Pitch cap x pitches per out: the ceiling on outs is cap divided by pitches per out, so the cap and efficiency (and opponent patience) interact and determine the upper tail.
Performance-triggered hook: early runs and baserunners trigger pulls, so run-prevention quality, contact allowed and manager hook policy interact to create the left tail of outs.
Bullpen state x leash: a depleted bullpen lengthens the starter's leash while a rested bullpen and analytics-driven manager shorten it before the third trip.
Opener flag x listed pitcher: opener usage collapses outs (and may void), so probable-pitcher status must gate every other input.

The outs ceiling equals the pitch cap divided by pitches per out, so for capped starters (rehab, innings limit) the cap is binding and the opponent's patience determines which rung the ceiling falls on; for uncapped starters the cap never binds and patience only matters through the performance hook. The effect is a regime switch on whether cap/(pitches per out) falls below the rung.

Managers who pull at the start of the third trip remove starters at outs 18 and nearly never at 19-20, while fresh bullpens raise the probability a hook is pulled at the boundary. The rung P(outs>=19) therefore depends on the boundary decision rather than on running performance, and the dependence is on the bullpen state in discrete steps.

Early runs convert contact allowed into a pull: a starter with weak contact suppression who allows a first-inning crooked number is removed early, so the same quality gap shows up as a left-tail mass rather than a shift of the mean. The hook response is conditional on runs allowed to date, not on pregame quality alone.

Ground-ball pitchers earn extra outs by double plays when a runner is on first, but only in lineups that put runners on and hit grounders; strikeout pitchers earn no DP outs. Outs per BF is therefore a product of GB share, traffic on first and lineup DP rate rather than an additive pitcher quality term.

A weather delay matters only when the roof is open and rain overlaps the middle innings; given a delay over an hour the starter usually does not return, so the effect on outs is conditional on both timing and length, truncating the right tail only in wet parks.

Outs recorded are pitch budget divided by pitches per out, and pitches per out is pitches per PA divided by outs per PA: a lineup with low out rate raises pitches per out and pulls the pitch ceiling down, so lineup out-rate and pitch efficiency multiply through the cap rather than adding.

pitcher_outs.label: Starting pitcher outs recorded (innings pitched) thresholds
pitcher_outs.mechanism: Outs = batters faced x probability each PA ends in at least one out, so the outcome is the workload distribution times (1 - on-base rate allowed) and is capped by the pitch limit and the manager's hook. Unlike strikeouts, outs are highly sensitive to run prevention in-game (a bad inning triggers an early pull) and to pitcher efficiency (pitches per out), so the distribution is left-skewed with a mass of early exits and a ceiling near the cap. The key information is pitch cap, hook policy, run-prevention quality and the opponent's on-base skills; realised pitch count is unknown before the game.
pitcher_outs.target: Whether the starter records at least k outs (e.g. 15 outs = five innings), requiring the pitcher to start per the wording.

inputs.why: Baseline pitcher K%/CSW/whiff regressed and opposing lineup K% by handedness.
Pitch-by-pitch whiff and putaway rates by batter hand identify where Ks come from, and which pitches the starter will lean on.
Confirmed batting order's whiff rates against the pitcher's pitch types convert arsenal into a lineup-specific K expectation.
Confirmed-lineup K% against the pitcher's hand, weighted by PA slot, replaces team-average K%.
Usage by count and handedness, velocity and chase rates describe the mechanism and detect changes in arsenal.
Expected batters faced multiplies per-PA K probability; workload variance is often larger than rate uncertainty.
Run differential and pitch count drive the early hook that truncates strikeout opportunity.
Returning-from-injury or workload caps create a hard ceiling on batters faced.
Pitches per PA convert pitch cap into batters faced; strikeouts cost extra pitches.
Patient lineups run up pitch counts and may shorten outings while whiffing less on pitches out of the zone.
Third-time-through penalty reduces per-PA K and raises hook probability late in the outing.
Umpire's called-strike zone shifts K and BB probabilities for the game.
Umpire K%/BB% over expected adjusted for pitcher/batter mix gives magnitude for the zone effect.
Catcher receiving changes called-strike rate on borderline pitches; backup catchers alter the environment.
Velocity or spin decline flags fatigue or injury and predicts lower whiff and earlier exit.
Opener/bullpen game flags make the listed pitcher's batters faced tiny or the market void.
Bullpen availability and fatigue change how long the manager lets the starter go.
Park and altitude influence pitch movement and K rates modestly and pitch count via run environment.
Cold weather lowers velocity and spin, hot weather helps contact carry; effect on whiff is small but plausible.
Handedness composition of the lineup (and switch hitters) determines which pitch types are effective.
Late scratches in the lineup change the K mix; pitcher scratch voids or reprices the market.
Strikeout rungs must imply a coherent distribution; stale rungs after lineup news can be detected.
Settlement wording on starter requirement, innings and voids.
Price move after lineup confirmation and umpire assignment reveals how the market incorporated the news.

Strikeout rungs at 8+ to 10+ are sensitive to which sub-event drives a pitcher's K%, and a lineup of patient fouling hitters is a different test than a lineup of free swingers; this keeps the matchup count-state-aware.

The Kalshi ladder pays on the right tail of strikeouts, and the right tail is exit-time driven; a hazard curve makes the hook policy of this manager and this bullpen state an explicit, testable factor.
Rungs are nested thresholds on one count; without the dispersion parameter the model cannot price both tails of the ladder consistently.
A backup catcher can shift the called-strike share enough to move a 7+/8+ rung, and the information arrives with the lineup.
Adds the missing 2026+ zone mechanism for strikeout ladders, where called third strikes and count leverage are central.

interactions.hypothesis: Pitch mix x lineup whiff by pitch: K rate = sum over pitch types of usage x pitcher whiff x lineup whiff relative to league on that pitch; a slider-heavy pitcher against a lineup weak vs sliders is worth more than aggregate K% suggests.

Times-through-order x hook: K per BF declines each trip while survival to later trips depends on pitch count and leash, so expected K is a survival-weighted sum across trips and a short leash cuts the high-K tail.

Umpire zone x called-strike rate x framing: a wide zone adds called strikes mainly for pitchers who work the edges and with strong framing, so the umpire adjustment should be scaled by the pitcher's edge/called-strike share.

Platoon x pitch mix x confirmed lineup: lineup handedness determines whether the changeup (vs opposite-hand) or the breaking ball (vs same-hand) is used, so lineup handedness composition shifts the pitch mix, and hence K%.

Pitch cap x efficiency x opponent patience: batters faced = cap / pitches per PA, where P/PA depends on both pitcher efficiency and lineup patience, so cap and patience must be modelled jointly (and a high-K strategy is pitch-expensive).
Velocity trend x leash: a pitcher with falling velocity gets pulled earlier by performance, so velocity signals should adjust both per-PA K and exit probability.

A high-strikeout style raises the number of two-strike pitches and fouls, so the same pitcher who gains Ks per batter also spends more pitches per batter and survives fewer batters. Strikeouts and batters faced are therefore negatively coupled through the pitch budget, and the coupling is strongest against patient lineups that foul off two-strike pitches.

The contract settles an opener on the small count but settles a scratch at the undefined fair market price, so the distribution is a mixture over three regimes whose weights move with news. The hazard curve differs by regime (about 3-4 batters for an opener versus a normal starter curve), and the mixture weight, not the performance model, dominates high-rung probability whenever opener risk is above a few percent.

Called strikes contribute only to the looking-strikeout share of a pitcher's Ks, so a wider zone and a better framer help most the pitchers who live on the edges and hurt least those who get strikeouts swinging. Adjustments must be scaled by the pitcher's looking-K share rather than added flat. Under the 2026 ABS challenge regime the zone effect is partially overridden on challenged edge pitches, so the interaction must be estimated with a regime flag and shrunk umpire/framing coefficients.

On the second and third trips pitchers lean away from their best pitch and hitters have seen it, so the effective whiff rate steps down at batter 19 and 28 while lineup whiff by pitch type changes sign of importance (the offspeed whiff matters more later). The decay is a step at trip boundaries, not smooth in batters faced.

Start-level latent quality widens the K distribution as batters faced grows (variance of a correlated sum scales with BF squared), so on long outings a good day produces 11+ Ks far more often than independence implies. Early velocity relative to baseline is the only pregame-adjacent signal of the latent state.

pitcher_strikeouts.label: Starting pitcher strikeouts thresholds
pitcher_strikeouts.mechanism: Expected strikeouts = expected batters faced x expected per-PA strikeout probability, summed over trips through the order. Per-PA K probability combines the pitcher's pitch-by-pitch swing-and-miss and called-strike skill (weighted by the pitch mix he uses against each batter handedness and in two-strike counts) with the confirmed lineup's whiff/K tendencies against those pitch types and handedness, then shifts with the umpire's zone, catcher framing, park/weather (velocity, movement) and the times-through-order penalty. Batters faced is capped by pitch count divided by pitches per PA and by the manager's hook, which depends on score, bullpen state and performance; realised pitch count is not knowable pregame, so the model is a mixture over exit scenarios and the outputs are a full count distribution, not a mean.
pitcher_strikeouts.target: Whether the listed starter records at least k strikeouts in the game (ladder of rungs), conditional on starting per the contract wording.

inputs.why: Lineup card timing and confirmation.
Starter/platoon/bench role: a player's role determines whether he starts and how many PAs he gets, which drives participation and counting-stat markets.
Rest after night games and travel.
IL status and late scratches: absences change lineup/rotation composition and late scratches can void or reprice player markets.
Manager platoon and substitution style.
Schedule density and doubleheaders.
Opposing starter handedness drives platoon sits.
Beat-writer reports on availability.
Definition of plays/starts and void rules.
Lineup posting vs market close.
Clinched or eliminated teams rest regulars and call up prospects; the policy is manager-specific and timestamped by announcement.
The contract's No-on-replacement rule makes this hazard a term in the price after the card posts.
KXMLBPITCH and similar windows depend on rehab timing rather than games played.
Converts single-game probabilities to window-level probability with correct correlation structure.
Gives the starting-pitcher participation market a rotation-based mechanism instead of the hitter lineup chain.
Defines the missing call-up inputs for the debut series.

interactions.hypothesis: Rest pattern x opposing handedness: platoon players sit against same-handed starters, so P(start) combines rest-day pattern and the starter's handedness.
Lineup posting time x market close: probabilities are mixtures until the card posts, so the posting timestamp relative to close defines the information advantage.
Injury vintage x scratch risk: players listed day-to-day have elevated scratch probability late, so injury reports and warm-up news interact with lineup confirmation.

A platoon player sits against same-handed starters and rests after night games, so start probability is a conditional product of role, opposing hand and rest pattern; for everyday players only the rest pattern matters, so the effect of handedness is gated by role.

Before the card posts the probability is a mixture of manager patterns, after posting it collapses to the scratch hazard; the transition is a step in time at posting, so the value of information is concentrated at posting relative to market close.

Window availability is a survival process: rehab stage determines time to activation, injury hazard after activation determines early failure, and the number of games available determines how many opportunities there are; failures across games are correlated through the absorbing state.

After a team clinches a seed or is eliminated, rest probability switches regime: regulars sit and prospects play, with the size of the switch depending on the manager's style and on whether seeding still matters; before clinching the baseline pattern applies.

Role changes (call-up, trade, injury replacement) announced by news shift start probability at a discrete date, so the window model must restart its per-game probabilities at the change; the number of games after the change drives the window probability.

For a returning starting pitcher the window market is Yes only if activation comes early enough for a rotation turn inside the window: activation two days before the window ends may produce no appearance if his slot falls after it, whereas a position player activated the same day usually enters at once, so the same rehab stage implies different window probabilities by role.

player_participation.label: Player participation (plays / starts / appears)
player_participation.mechanism: Participation is determined by manager decisions (rest days, platoon sits), injury status and late scratches, resolved mostly when the lineup card posts; before then it is a probability from rest-day patterns, handedness of the opposing starter and injury news, afterwards it is near-certain except for in-game substitution cases. The edge is timing relative to market close and the exact definition (starts vs appears).
player_participation.target: Whether a named player plays or starts in a game, per the contract's definition.

inputs.why: Monte Carlo of the remaining schedule and bracket.
Talent prior from projection systems.
Regress record luck to run differential.
Remaining schedule quality: future opponent quality, home/away split and days off shape expected wins for the remainder of the season.
Injuries to key players and depth.
Rotation quality, especially in October.
Bullpen quality for close games.
Seeding and tiebreaker rules: seeding, wild-card format and tiebreaker rules decide who plays whom and with what home field, determining futures settle paths.
Series state, rest and rotation for series markets.
Postseason pitching usage patterns.
League baselines for season specials.
Trades and call-ups: transactions and news change who plays and the team's strength with a lag before statistics catch up.
Futures benchmark: sharp sportsbook and exchange lines are a competing aggregation of information and the standard benchmark for fair probability.
Division, wildcard and win-total markets are tails of a schedule simulation with injury and rating uncertainty.
Provides the tail-width parameter the season simulation needs.
Seed and qualifier markets settle on seed and bracket, so ignoring tiebreakers misprices close races.
Matches the information relevant to series and title futures instead of full-season ratings.
A direct input to the remaining-schedule simulation that is not captured by season-to-date records.
Supplies the primary state of the win-total ladders that pythag_luck alone did not define.
Specifies the missing inputs for the matchup and games-hosted series.
Gives series MVP series a defined model instead of a market-price input.
Defines exposure for the playoff leader series, which previously had no inputs.
Gives KXMLBWORLD a national-team strength input; no club-level input in this archetype measures it.

interactions.hypothesis: Talent uncertainty x series length: greater uncertainty about true strength widens futures outcomes and short series compress the talent gap, so rating uncertainty and format interact.
Luck regression x tiebreakers: simulation should use expected wins for strength but formal tiebreakers for the ties, so regress luck first, apply rules second.
Injury state x remaining schedule: a long-term injury reduces strength for the remainder, with a larger effect when remaining opponents are strong or the margin for playoffs is thin.

The weight on run-based evidence versus the preseason prior is games/(games + k), so early in the season the prior dominates and late the record dominates; the posterior variance falls accordingly. The interaction between games played and each source determines tail width, so the two sources cannot be added with fixed weights.

A seller's loss of rest-of-season WAR matters most for teams still in the race, and its effect on win total is proportional to games remaining; opponent strength of those remaining games conditions the impact on wins, so the shift must enter the simulation, not the record.

Championship probability is convex in seed through the bye and bracket: a top-two division winner skips a round (one fewer series to win) and faces weaker opponents; the value of one extra win near the seeding boundary is large, so final-week wins have convex impact on title odds.

In the postseason the rotation shortens, so the weight on top starters rises and day-by-day starter identity matters; the pitching regime changes at the start of the playoffs, so regular-season starter weights misprice series.

Uncertainty about team strength is shared across games and rounds, so series outcomes are positively correlated across a team's path: a team that is stronger than believed wins several series, which fattens the tails of championship probability relative to independent rounds.

The chance of a long streak rises much faster than linearly in per-game win probability (P of an L-game run scales like p^L), so the strongest teams dominate the streak market more than their win-total edge suggests, and a team with an active streak near the league maximum late in the season is priced mostly off its next few games; games remaining cap the opportunity.

For 2027 futures the model is a mixture over labour regimes: no stoppage (a normal 162-game season), a shortened season (fewer games, so more variance in standings and more upsets of strong teams) and a cancelled postseason (settlement unknown). Strong favourites lose value under shortened seasons because season-long talent edges matter less, so the regime weights interact with team strength rather than scaling all teams equally.

Best-record, worst-record and 100-loss outcomes are linked: teams share opponents, so one team's extra wins are another's losses, and the worst-record race is usually decided among two or three teams whose posteriors overlap. Ties at the extreme pay $1/N, so the joint probability of equal winning percentages near the end of the season changes expected payouts even when the leader is clear.

season_futures.label: Division winner, season wins, postseason futures and series
season_futures.mechanism: Futures integrate talent estimates (projection priors updated with run differential, not record) through the remaining schedule with uncertainty, then apply tiebreakers and bracket rules; postseason series switch to a game-level dynamic program using announced starters, rest, bullpen usage and home-field pattern. Long-horizon prices depend on rating uncertainty and slow information (injuries, trades); short-horizon series prices depend on pitching availability and shortened managerial hooks. Luck regression and tiebreaker formalities matter most in close races.
season_futures.target: Team season outcomes: division title, win total thresholds, playoff/pennant/title futures, postseason series winners, records and specials.

interactions.hypothesis: Rate x opportunity x availability: final total = current + rate x games remaining x P(play), so injury hazard and role changes interact with talent for leaders.
Qualification x rate stats: borderline players qualify only by PA accrual, so playing time and qualification rules interact in batting-average or ERA leader markets.
Production rank x team success x ballot timing: voters weigh WAR with team outcome and cast ballots at a specific time, so late-season changes matter only before the deadline.

Final total equals current plus rate times games remaining times the probability of playing, so injury hazard and role changes scale the projected increment; for a leader with a small lead and a high injury risk, availability dominates talent differences.

Rate-stat leaders need the plate-appearance qualification (3.1 PA per scheduled team game for batters), so a borderline hitter's probability of leading a rate category depends on whether he accrues enough PAs; just below the threshold the official shortfall provision still lets him lead if hitless at-bats added up to the minimum leave his rate on top, so the threshold is soft for batters. No equivalent provision is known for the ERA title (1 inning per team game), which stays a hard cut (unverified; contract wording unseen).

Voters trade off WAR and narrative and team success nonlinearly: beyond a certain WAR gap the narrative matters little, and below it a division title can flip the ranking; the interaction between production gap and team success is not additive.

Finalist markets settle on a top-three rank only if finalists are announced before the winner. The rank event and the announcement-timing event are different processes; the interaction of interest is whether announcement timing depends on how tight the field is or on the award's calendar, not their product.

Triple Crown needs one player to lead three correlated stats; the joint probability depends on the covariance of HR and RBI (strongly positive) and AVG (weakly related), so the probability is much larger than an independent product for a power hitter with a big lead but small when AVG is contested. The stated covariances and the 1.5-sd collapse are illustrative and must be estimated.

A series-MVP or playoff-leader probability is the product of team advancement (games played) and the player's share of production or credit given those games; the same hitter is a long shot if his team is likely to be swept and a favourite if a seven-game series is likely, so team and player components cannot be added.

A staff's strikeout lead depends on who pitches the remaining innings: a deadline acquisition of a high-strikeout starter or the loss of an ace to injury shifts the staff K% for the rest of the season, and the effect on the leader market is large only when the race is close, since a staff ahead by a hundred strikeouts in August is rarely caught.

season_leaders_and_awards.label: Season leaders, player stat totals and awards
season_leaders_and_awards.mechanism: Season-stat and leader outcomes are current total plus rest-of-season rate times opportunity times availability, so a competitor-level simulation (with correlated team context, injury risk, and qualification rules for rate stats) gives probabilities. Awards add a voter model: production rank, team success and narrative under a specific ballot structure and timing, with finalists as information events. Early-season leaders mostly reflect luck, so regressing rates is the main lever, while late-season markets are dominated by games remaining and injuries.
season_leaders_and_awards.target: Leader of a statistical category, a player's season total threshold, or winner of an award (MVP, Cy Young, ROY).

Team standing drives trade behaviour.
Option, 40-man and Rule 5 constraints.

Injuries trigger call-ups and IL moves.
Playoff odds define buyer/seller state.
Reference-class frequencies: for off-field markets, history of similar announcements is the best available prior.
What counts as an official transaction.
Market reaction to reports: the traded price aggregates every participant's information about this contract, including injury and lineup news that moves faster than public stats.
Defines feasibility and timing, which are first-order for next-team markets.
Provides the likelihood ratio for the most important information type.
Gives time-conditioned base rates instead of one reference-class rate.
Explains who can sign or trade for salary and so conditions signing and trade probabilities.

Adds the selection stage the record lacked: the markets are one-per-team and one-per-candidate.
Adds the missing labour-stoppage regime for transactions whose windows span Dec 1 2026.
